title: The British Expedition to Abyssinia: An Emperor Seizes Every Diplomat
dek: Victoria never answered one letter, so Tewodros II locked the British consul and a batch of missionaries inside Magdala at the top of a mountain — and got an expeditionary force instead.
why: The first half is a long build, but the second half is extraordinarily dense with the hostage crisis and the emperor's psychological collapse — good for listeners interested in imperial history and negotiation as a game.
who: Listeners interested in Victorian imperial history, hostage negotiation, and the psychology of paranoid leaders; anyone who wants to understand how Britain went from diplomatic failure to military expedition.
skip: The opening Flashman novel quotation and the Canadian listener joke can be skipped; start at 07:13 when Plowden appears.

points.h: One unanswered letter lit the war
points.body: Tewodros II wrote Victoria a letter phrased like a pen pal: ‘How are you? I am well, thank God.’ The letter travelled via the Red Sea, Aden, Bombay, Suez, Alexandria, Marseille and London — halfway around the world — and ended up filed by the Foreign Office in the India Office records. No one replied. The emperor waited two years, and his expectation turned to suspicion that Britain was colluding with his Muslim enemies. In 1864 he seized the British consul Cameron and a group of missionaries, and the hostage crisis began.

points.h: He claimed Solomonic descent, and meant it
points.body: Abyssinia had a legend: a descendant of Solomon and David would rise, unify the divided kingdom, defeat the Egyptians, and march all the way to Jerusalem, and his name would be Tewodros. In 1855 Kasa — of obscure origin, a former bandit chief — defeated his last rival, declared himself the new emperor, and took the name Tewodros II. He later claimed Solomonic descent, though Plowden records no such claim at their first meeting. This messianic identity was both the source of his legitimacy and the root of his later paranoia.

points.h: After his wife died he began to lose control
points.body: In 1858 Tewodros's wife Tewabech died, and he was grief-stricken. His next wife, the 12-year-old Tiruwork, was cold to him and said, ‘I am speaking with a king greater than you — get out.’ He began drinking heavily, sleeping with women in the camp at random, and admitted to the missionaries that he was living ‘a very unchristian and indecent life.’ In 1860 his friend Plowden was ambushed by rebels and died nine days after being speared. Britain sent a new representative only two years later, and in the interval the emperor's paranoia deteriorated sharply.

points.h: The letter Cameron carried became the fuse
points.body: At the end of 1862, when Cameron left the emperor's camp, he took with him a letter in which Tewodros asked Victoria to arrange safe passage for his envoys and said, ‘See how Islam oppresses the Christians.’ Cameron came back saying he had received no reply from London, and the emperor began to suspect he had gone off to Sudan to collude with the Muslims. In October 1863 the missionary Stern angered the emperor by publishing Wanderings Among the Falashas, and was arrested, whipped and put in chains. In January 1864 Cameron and the other missionaries were seized too, and all the hostages realised the nightmare had only just begun.

points.h: What Britain really feared was France
points.body: The Foreign Office did not particularly care whether the missionaries lived or died; what worried them was France. Suez Canal fever was at its height, and if they alienated Tewodros he might turn to Paris, giving France control of the route from the Red Sea to India. So they sent Hormuzd Rassam — a Mosul-born Assyrian, archaeologist, discoverer of Ashurbanipal's palace and the Epic of Gilgamesh, Oxford-educated, a Protestant convert, and an ardent Anglophile. He set out for Abyssinia with Victoria's letter and two assistants, Dr Blanc and Lieutenant Prideaux.

points.h: Rassam nearly succeeded, then was seized
points.body: In January 1866 Rassam met Tewodros in his blue diplomatic uniform, and after reading Victoria's letter the emperor was so excited he could not sleep; the next day he dictated a reply calling the queen ‘the defender of the religion chosen by God.’ He agreed to release all the hostages, but demanded that Rassam first accompany him on a campaign to put down a rebellion. Along the way the emperor kept sending gifts: muskets, manuscripts, salmon, antelopes, two lion cubs, two monkeys and a baboon. In March 1866 the hostages were finally brought to the lake, but on 13 April, when Rassam came to say goodbye, he found that he too had been arrested.

points.h: He held them all for gunsmiths alone
points.body: Why did Tewodros seize Rassam? There are three possibilities: he had been acting the whole time; he was overcome at the last moment by his hatred of the missionaries; or he genuinely liked Rassam and could not bear to let him go. Philip Marsden thinks the third most likely — the emperor was infatuated with Rassam and saw him as his only channel to British friendship and British technology. The emperor then wrote to Victoria demanding ‘skilled craftsmen, blacksmiths, gunsmiths, artillery experts’ to make guns, and said he would release the hostages once he was satisfied.

points.h: In the cellar he admitted he was mad
points.body: Tewodros locked the missionaries in a cellar and came in with a bottle of arak, sat down among them, and drank and talked. At last he said, calmly and sorrowfully: ‘My father was mad. People often said I was mad, and I never believed them. But now I know it is true.’ Rassam urged him not to say such things, and the emperor walked to the door, turned back, and said in a hoarse whisper: ‘I am mad. Goodbye.’ Then he left. For nearly two years after that they were held on the mountain of Magdala, at ten thousand feet, in chains, their spines bent.
